lesson.title: The Raid That Set Virginia's Nerves on Fire: Harpers Ferry, 1859
lesson.summary: In October 1859, radical abolitionist John Brown led a small armed band in a failed attempt to seize a federal arsenal and spark a slave uprising, an act that hardened both Northern and Southern opinion in the last years before the Civil War.
lesson.body:
John Brown had already earned a reputation as a violent abolitionist before he ever set foot in Harpers Ferry. During the fighting in Kansas Territory known as Bleeding Kansas, Brown and several of his sons killed five pro-slavery settlers along Pottawatomie Creek in May 1856, convinced that only force, not petitions or votes, could stop the spread of slavery into the western territories. That conviction only deepened over the next three years, and by 1859 Brown had settled on a far more ambitious plan: seize the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, arm the enslaved people of the surrounding countryside, and touch off a widening rebellion that would spread south through the Appalachians.

On the night of October 16, 1859, Brown led twenty one men, including five Black raiders, Dangerfield Newby, Osborne Anderson, Shields Green, Lewis Sheridan Leary, and John Copeland, into the town and captured the arsenal with little resistance. But the uprising he expected never came. Word spread quickly, local militia and armed townspeople surrounded the engine house where Brown and his remaining men had barricaded themselves, and by October 18 a detachment of United States Marines commanded by Colonel Robert E. Lee, with Lieutenant J.E.B. Stuart at his side, stormed the building and captured Brown, who was wounded in the fighting. Ten of the raiders, including two of Brown's sons, were killed.

Virginia tried Brown swiftly on charges of treason against the state, conspiracy, and murder. He was convicted and hanged in Charles Town on December 2, 1859, and he faced the gallows with a calm that many Northerners, even those who had never supported his methods, found genuinely striking. His funding had come partly from a group of wealthy Northern abolitionists later called the Secret Six, and while most Republican politicians, including Abraham Lincoln, publicly distanced themselves from Brown's violence, church bells tolled and memorial meetings were held across parts of the North on the day of his execution.

The raid's real power was in how differently it was read in each section of the country. Southerners saw confirmation of their worst fear: that Northern abolitionists were actively conspiring to arm enslaved people and slaughter white families, and state legislatures across the South poured money into militias in response. Many Northerners, meanwhile, came to see Brown less as a criminal than as a martyr for a righteous cause, a shift that alarmed Southern moderates who had hoped sectional tensions might still be managed through compromise. Harpers Ferry did not cause the Civil War by itself, but it stripped away the assumption, on both sides, that the other section could still be reasoned with, and it set the emotional stage for the presidential election that would follow less than a year later.
